title: Cost of Debt Financing and Corporate Investment in the EU-27: Deleveraging and Profit Buffers Under Monetary Tightening
content: The rise in the cost of financing after 2022 constitutes a substantial interest rate test of the financial resilience of European non-financial corporations following a prolonged period of exceptionally cheap debt. This paper examines how changes in the cost of debt financing affect corporate investment in the EU-27 and the extent to which this effect depends on the leverage and profit buffers of firms. The analysis draws on harmonised data from the Eurostat sector accounts, compiled under the ESA 2010 methodology (European Union, 2010), for the period 2000-2025. Three main indicators are examined: the gross investment rate, the gross profit share, and the ratio of net debt to income. The empirical approach combines panel models with country and year fixed effects and local projections. The results show that what matters for corporate investment is above all the real, rather than the nominal, cost of debt. A higher real cost of debt financing is associated with a lower investment rate, but this effect weakens in the period after 2020. At the same time, European non-financial corporations enter the most recent episode of monetary tightening with stronger balance sheets: the average ratio of net debt to income falls from around 477% in the crisis years to around 226% during the tightening period, with a relatively stable profit share of around 44% of gross value added. The local projections show that the effect of the real cost of debt on investment is strongest immediately after the shock and gradually weakens within two to three years. This implies that more expensive financing postpones part of investment rather than reducing it permanently. The results also indicate that prior deleveraging and the accumulated profit buffers have probably made European non-financial corporations more resilient to the most recent episode of monetary tightening. The paper contributes to the literature on corporate investment and capital structure by showing that the financial condition of firms matters for the way in which they respond to changes in the cost of financing.
